title: REG U3·W4 — Tax-Exempt Organizations (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — when an entity pays no income tax

If Jordan Reed endows a family foundation or MBG supports a local charity, a different creature appears: a tax-exempt organization that pays no federal income tax on income furthering its exempt purpose. Exemption is a privilege with strings — strict organizational rules, prohibited activities, special taxes on private foundations, and a tax on business income unrelated to the mission. This closes REG Unit 3.

Qualifying under §501(c)(3)

The best-known exemption, §501(c)(3), covers organizations organized and operated exclusively for charitable, religious, educational, scientific, or literary purposes. Two tests must both be met: the organizational test (the governing documents limit the entity to exempt purposes and dedicate assets to charity on dissolution) and the operational test (it actually operates that way). A §501(c)(3) is uniquely valuable because contributions to it are tax-deductible to donors.

The prohibited activities

Exemption is lost or penalized for three things. Private inurement — letting the organization's earnings benefit insiders (excess compensation, sweetheart deals) — is strictly forbidden, and excess benefit transactions trigger intermediate-sanction excise taxes on the insiders. Lobbying must be insubstantial (or within a measured election). And political campaign activity — supporting or opposing a candidate — is an absolute prohibition for a §501(c)(3); even a single endorsement can cost the exemption.

Applying for recognition

An organization seeks recognition of exemption by filing Form 1023 (a streamlined 1023-EZ exists for small organizations). The IRS issues a determination letter. While churches and very small organizations have relief from applying, recognition is what assures donors their gifts are deductible and the entity is exempt — so most file. Recognition is prospective discipline, not a one-time pass: the entity must keep meeting the operational test.

Public charity versus private foundation

Every §501(c)(3) is presumed a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity — typically by passing a public support test (drawing a broad base of public donations) or by being an inherently public institution like a church, school, or hospital. The distinction matters greatly: private foundations (such as Reed's family foundation, funded by one family) face a battery of excise taxes and tighter rules that public charities escape.

Private foundation excise taxes

Private foundations bear special excise taxes designed to force charitable use and prevent abuse: a tax on net investment income; a penalty for failing to make the required minimum distributions (roughly 5% of investment assets) for charitable purposes each year; prohibitions on self-dealing between the foundation and its insiders; limits on excess business holdings (owning too much of a business); and taxes on jeopardizing investments and improper taxable expenditures (such as lobbying). These rules are why a family foundation is more tightly regulated than a community public charity.

Unrelated business income tax (UBIT)

Even an exempt organization pays regular corporate tax — UBIT, reported on Form 990-T — on income from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and not substantially related to its exempt purpose. The classic example: a charity that runs a commercial business unrelated to its mission. Debt-financed income is also taxed. But key exceptions remove income produced by substantially all volunteer labor, the sale of donated goods, or activities run for the convenience of members (a hospital cafeteria) — and passive dividends, interest, and rents are generally excluded. UBIT keeps tax-exempt entities from competing untaxed with ordinary businesses.

Annual compliance and other exempt types

Most exempt organizations file an annual information return — Form 990 (with 990-EZ and the postcard 990-N for smaller groups; private foundations file 990-PF). Failing to file for three consecutive years automatically revokes exemption. Beyond §501(c)(3), other categories exist — §501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations (which may lobby and do limited political work, but gifts are not deductible) and §501(c)(6) trade associations and chambers of commerce, the kind a construction industry group would use. Each is exempt, but only the §501(c)(3) offers donors a deduction.

Intermediate sanctions and donor substantiation

Two compliance points round out §501(c)(3) practice. Rather than revoking exemption for every insider abuse, the IRS can impose intermediate sanctions — excise taxes on a disqualified person who receives an excess benefit (and on managers who knowingly approve it) — a more proportionate remedy than killing the charity. And to claim a deduction, donors must meet substantiation rules: a contemporaneous written acknowledgment for any gift of $250 or more, additional appraisal requirements for larger noncash gifts, and disclosure on the receipt of the value of any goods or services the donor received in return (the quid pro quo rule). A charity that fails to provide these disclosures can itself be penalized — tying the exempt entity's compliance directly to its donors' deductions.

Choosing among the exempt categories

Not every mission fits §501(c)(3). A §501(c)(4) social-welfare organization may engage in substantial lobbying and some political activity that a charity cannot, but contributions to it are not deductible — a trade-off advocacy groups accept. A §501(c)(6) business league, trade association, or chamber of commerce serves a common business interest (a construction-contractors association, say); member dues may be deductible as a business expense, though the portion used for lobbying is not. §501(c)(7) social clubs round out the common list. The throughline of REG Unit 3 is that the tax law follows the purpose of a transfer or an entity — income earned, value transferred at gift or death, or income devoted to charity — taxing each once under its own regime, leaving the planner to route value through the regime that serves the family and the mission at the least tax.

State registration and the compliance calendar

Exempt status is federal, but an organization must also register and report under state charity and solicitation laws and maintain the governance records the §990 makes public — board minutes, a conflict-of-interest policy, and documented compensation approvals. The §990 has itself become a transparency document: it discloses program-versus-overhead spending, the highest-paid people, and related-party transactions, so the form a charity files is in practice its public accountability statement. For a family foundation like Reed's the calendar is unforgiving — the annual 990-PF, the excise-tax computation on net investment income, and the yearly 5% minimum distribution must all be met, and a lapse converts the privilege of exemption into penalties. Exemption, in short, is earned every year, not granted once.

CMA bridge

CMA's ethics and governance themes reappear here as the law of the nonprofit sector: the private-inurement bar and self-dealing rules are the legal backbone of the tone-at-the-top controls a foundation's board must keep — and the §990 information return is the public's window into how an exempt organization actually spends its money.

Practice and recap

  1. Qualify under §501(c)(3) by meeting the organizational and operational tests; contributions are deductible only to (c)(3) organizations.
  2. Avoid private inurement, keep lobbying insubstantial, and never engage in political campaign activity.
  3. Distinguish public charities (public support test) from private foundations, which bear net-investment-income, minimum-distribution, self-dealing, and excess-business-holdings excise taxes.
  4. Pay UBIT (Form 990-T) on regularly carried-on unrelated business income and debt-financed income; file the annual Form 990 (three missed years revokes exemption).

Recap: a §501(c)(3) must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes, avoid private inurement and political activity, and offers donors a deduction; private foundations face extra excise taxes (net investment income, 5% minimum distribution, self-dealing, excess business holdings) that public charities escape; UBIT taxes unrelated, regularly carried-on business income; and the annual Form 990 is the compliance backbone — three missed filings revoke the exemption.

flashcards.back: Organized AND operated exclusively for charitable/religious/educational/scientific purposes; meets the organizational and operational tests. Contributions are tax-deductible.
Private inurement (insider benefit), more-than-insubstantial lobbying, and ANY political campaign activity (absolute bar).
File Form 1023 (or 1023-EZ for small orgs); the IRS issues a determination letter.
Every (c)(3) is a private foundation unless it passes a public support test or is an inherently public institution (church/school/hospital).
Net investment income tax, ~5% minimum-distribution requirement, self-dealing, excess business holdings, jeopardizing investments, and taxable expenditures.
Regular tax (Form 990-T) on a trade/business regularly carried on and not substantially related to the exempt purpose; debt-financed income too.
Volunteer labor, sale of donated goods, member-convenience activities, and passive dividends/interest/rents are generally excluded.
Form 990 series (990/990-EZ/990-N; 990-PF for foundations); failing to file for 3 consecutive years revokes exemption.

questions.q: Contributions are tax-deductible to the donor when made to which organization?
questions.explain: Only §501(c)(3) organizations offer donors a charitable contribution deduction.

questions.q: Which activity is ABSOLUTELY prohibited for a §501(c)(3)?
choices: Political campaign activity for or against a candidate
questions.explain: Campaign intervention is an absolute bar; lobbying need only be insubstantial.

questions.q: Every §501(c)(3) is presumed to be a private foundation unless it:
choices: Qualifies as a public charity (e.g., passes a public support test)
questions.explain: A (c)(3) is a private foundation unless it qualifies as a public charity via the public support test or its institutional type.

questions.q: Private foundations must generally distribute for charitable purposes at least about:
questions.explain: Foundations face a minimum-distribution requirement of roughly 5% of net investment assets each year.

questions.q: The unrelated business income tax (UBIT) applies to income from a trade or business that is:
choices: Regularly carried on and not substantially related to the exempt purpose
questions.explain: UBIT taxes regularly carried-on business income not substantially related to the exempt purpose (and debt-financed income).

choices: Income from a member-convenience activity such as a hospital cafeteria
A commercial business unrelated to the mission
questions.explain: Volunteer labor, donated-goods sales, and member-convenience activities are excepted from UBIT.

questions.q: An exempt organization that fails to file its annual return for three consecutive years:
choices: Owes a small late fee only
Is converted to a private foundation
questions.explain: Three consecutive years of non-filing automatically revokes tax-exempt status.
